cues.text: Let's work through an archived pre-test revision, covering two questions in order: Question 1 and Question 4.
First, Pre-test Question 1.
The question reads: Database management systems typically handle concurrency by, blank.
In other words, how does a database system cope when many users or programs work at the same time?
There are four options.
Option one: using control mechanisms to manage simultaneous transactions.
Option two: allowing only one user to access the system at a time.
Option three: ignoring transaction collisions and resolving manually.
Option four: deleting records automatically to free up locks.
The archived LMS correct answer is option one: using control mechanisms to manage simultaneous transactions.
Now, why does that make sense?
Concurrency simply means that several transactions are happening at the same moment.
A database can't just hope they won't interfere with each other, so it uses control mechanisms to coordinate them.
Notice the other options.
Allowing only one user at a time would avoid collisions, but it is not how database systems typically handle concurrency.
Ignoring collisions and fixing them manually is not a real strategy.
And deleting records to free up locks would destroy data, which is certainly not how locks are managed.
Next, Pre-test Question 4.
The question reads: Advanced database models help overcome traditional limitations by, blank.
Again there are four options.
Option one: supporting flat-file document processing in real-time.
Option two: enabling flexible schemas, distributed processing, and real-time analytics.
Option three: restricting replication across cloud systems for data security.
Option four: automatically removing data redundancy in all scenarios.
The archived LMS correct answer is option two: enabling flexible schemas, distributed processing, and real-time analytics.
Now let's pull the source's reasoning together.
For Question 1, the source says concurrency control coordinates simultaneous transactions while maintaining isolation.
Isolation means that each transaction behaves as though it is not being disturbed by the others running alongside it.
For Question 4, the source says advanced models offer flexible structures and distributed processing for appropriate workloads.
The important qualification is this: they do not guarantee removal of all redundancy.
That is exactly why option four is wrong.
The phrase "in all scenarios" claims too much, because advanced models do not promise to eliminate redundancy everywhere.
Keep that qualification in mind, because it is a classic way exam options are made to look attractive while being false.
